Cornwall: England's Sub-Tropical Motorcycle Destination

Cornwall occupies England's far south-west and has a character distinctly its own. The county has its own language (Kernewek), its own flag (St Piran's Cross), and a fierce independent identity. For motorcyclists, it offers dramatic Atlantic coastline, hidden coves, charming fishing harbours, and a climate mild enough for palm trees.

The North Coast

Cornwall's north coast faces the full force of the Atlantic and is correspondingly dramatic. Massive cliffs, surf beaches, and headlands create a raw, exciting landscape. Key destinations include Bude (excellent surfing town), Padstow (Rick Stein's foodie capital), Newquay (surf capital), and St Ives (artists' town with Tate gallery). The coast path offers cliff-top walks from every parking spot.

The South Coast

The south coast is gentler — sheltered harbours, sub-tropical gardens, and the calmer waters of the English Channel. Falmouth is a historic port with an excellent maritime museum. The Roseland Peninsula is one of Cornwall's best-kept secrets — quiet lanes through sub-tropical gardens. Fowey is a charming literary town (Daphne du Maurier country).

The Far West

Penwith, the far western tip, has a mystical quality. Ancient stone circles, Iron Age villages, and the remains of tin mining create a landscape steeped in history. The Minack Theatre — an open-air auditorium carved into the cliffs above Porthcurno — is one of the most spectacular performance venues in the world.

Cornwall is England's most visited county for good reason. Get off the main roads, explore the lanes, and you'll find the Cornwall that existed before the tourists arrived — timeless, beautiful, and utterly captivating.

Where to Stay

  • St Ives — Artists' town, Tate gallery, beautiful harbour beaches. Busy but essential
  • Padstow — Foodie paradise, excellent seafood restaurants, north coast base
  • Falmouth — University town with maritime heritage, south coast hub
  • Penzance — Gateway to Land's End and the Scilly Isles ferry, Art Deco lido
  • Boscastle — Dramatic harbour village, Thomas Hardy connections, north coast character

Practical Information

Cornwall is accessed via the A30 from Exeter or the A38 and A390 through Plymouth. Allow 5 hours from London, 4 from Birmingham. Fuel is available in all towns. The main roads (A30, A39) can be very congested in summer — arrive Friday evening or use the railway. Accommodation books up months in advance for July and August. Visit May-June or September-October for the best experience — warmer weather, fewer crowds, and lower prices. Read our Best Motorcycle Roads in Scotland: 15 Must-Ride Routes guide for more. faq.q: When is the best time to visit Cornwall by motorcycle?
faq.a: Visit in May-June or September-October for the best experience: warmer weather than the rest of England, fewer crowds and lower prices. Cornwall is extremely busy in July and August, when the A30, A39 and beach approaches become heavily congested. The county rarely gets snow, and spring arrives weeks earlier than up north.

faq.q: How do I get to Cornwall and how long does it take?
faq.a: Cornwall is accessed via the A30 from Exeter or the A38 and A390 through Plymouth. Allow about five hours from London and four from Birmingham. The main roads can be very congested in summer, so arrive on a Friday evening or consider using the railway to avoid the worst of the holiday traffic.

faq.q: What is the difference between Cornwall's north and south coasts?
faq.a: The north coast faces the full force of the Atlantic, with massive cliffs, surf beaches and dramatic headlands around Bude, Padstow, Newquay and St Ives. The south coast is gentler, with sheltered harbours, sub-tropical gardens and the calmer English Channel around Falmouth, the Roseland Peninsula and Fowey.

faq.q: Do I need to book accommodation in advance?
faq.a: Yes. Accommodation books up months in advance for July and August across Cornwall's popular towns such as St Ives, Padstow and Falmouth. If you visit in the shoulder seasons of May-June or September-October you will find more availability, lower prices and quieter roads to enjoy.

faq.q: What should I watch for when riding Cornish roads?
faq.a: Cornwall's narrow lanes and high hedges can be challenging, so approach blind bends cautiously as tractors, horses and campervans appear without warning. Watch for sand and gravel on coastal roads, especially after storms. Some remote areas have fuel stations with limited opening hours, so plan your refuelling.
